title: The Derivative as a Function
lead: Taking the derivative at every point at once gives a new function, the derivative function, written in several notations, Leibniz’s among them. Its graph is read from the graph of the function, its relation to continuity is settled, the ways a continuous function can fail to have a derivative are shown, and derivatives are taken again to give higher-order derivatives.
objectives: Define the derivative function of a given function.
Graph a derivative function from the graph of a given function.
State the connection between derivatives and continuity.
Describe three conditions for when a function does not have a derivative.
Explain the meaning of a higher-order derivative.
summary_html:
• The derivative of a function $\kf(x)$ is the function whose value at $x$ is $\kfprime(x).$
  • The graph of a derivative of a function $\kf(x)$ is related to the graph of $\kf(x).$ Where $\kf(x)$ has a tangent line with positive slope, $\kfprime(x)\gt 0.$ Where $\kf(x)$ has a tangent line with negative slope, $\kfprime(x)\lt 0.$ Where $\kf(x)$ has a horizontal tangent line, $\kfprime(x)=0.$
  • If a function is differentiable at a point, then it is continuous at that point. A function is not differentiable at a point if it is not continuous at the point, if it has a vertical tangent line at the point, or if the graph has a sharp corner or cusp.
  • Higher-order derivatives are derivatives of derivatives, from the second derivative to the $n\text{th}$ derivative.

For the following functions,

a. sketch the graph and

b. use the definition of a derivative to show that the function is not differentiable at $x=1.$

$f(x)=\{\begin{array}{l}2\sqrt{x},0\le x\le 1 \\ 3x-1,x\gt 1\end{array}$

answer.solution: a. The graph is the arc $y=2\sqrt{x}$ from $(0,0)$ up to $(1,2),$ then the line $y=3x-1,$ which starts at $(1,2)$ and rises with slope $3;$ the two pieces meet, so $f$ is continuous at $1.$ b. $f(1)=2.$ From the left, $\lim_{h\to 0^{-}}\frac{f(1+h)-f(1)}{h}=\lim_{h\to 0^{-}}\frac{2\sqrt{1+h}-2}{h}=\lim_{h\to 0^{-}}\frac{2((1+h)-1)}{h(\sqrt{1+h}+1)}=\lim_{h\to 0^{-}}\frac{2}{\sqrt{1+h}+1}=1.$ From the right, $\lim_{h\to 0^{+}}\frac{f(1+h)-f(1)}{h}=\lim_{h\to 0^{+}}\frac{3(1+h)-1-2}{h}=\lim_{h\to 0^{+}}\frac{3h}{h}=3.$ Since $1\ne 3,$ $\lim_{h\to 0}\frac{f(1+h)-f(1)}{h}$ does not exist, and $f$ is not differentiable at $x=1.$

exercises.prompt:
For the following functions,

a. sketch the graph and

b. use the definition of a derivative to show that the function is not differentiable at $x=1.$

$f(x)=\{\begin{array}{l}3,x\lt 1 \\ 3x,x\ge 1\end{array}$

answer.solution:
a.

b. $\lim_{h\to 0^{-}}\frac{f(1+h)-f(1)}{h}=\lim_{h\to 0^{-}}\frac{3-3}{h}=0$ $\lim_{h\to 0^{+}}\frac{f(1+h)-f(1)}{h}=\lim_{h\to 0^{+}}\frac{3(1+h)-3(1)}{h}=\lim_{h\to 0^{+}}\frac{3h}{h}=3$ $\lim_{h\to 0^{-}}\frac{f(1+h)-f(1)}{h}\ne \lim_{h\to 0^{+}}\frac{f(1+h)-f(1)}{h}$, so $\lim_{h\to 0}\frac{f(1+h)-f(1)}{h}$ does not exist.

exercises.prompt:
For the following functions,

a. sketch the graph and

b. use the definition of a derivative to show that the function is not differentiable at $x=1.$

$f(x)=\{\begin{array}{l}-x^{2}+2,x\le 1 \\ x,x\gt 1\end{array}$

answer.solution: a. The graph is the downward parabola $y=-x^{2}+2,$ with vertex $(0,2),$ up to the closed point $(1,1),$ then the line $y=x$ rising from $(1,1)$ with slope $1;$ the pieces meet, so $f$ is continuous at $1.$ b. $f(1)=1.$ From the left, $\lim_{h\to 0^{-}}\frac{f(1+h)-f(1)}{h}=\lim_{h\to 0^{-}}\frac{-(1+h)^{2}+2-1}{h}=\lim_{h\to 0^{-}}\frac{-2h-h^{2}}{h}=\lim_{h\to 0^{-}}(-2-h)=-2.$ From the right, $\lim_{h\to 0^{+}}\frac{f(1+h)-f(1)}{h}=\lim_{h\to 0^{+}}\frac{(1+h)-1}{h}=1.$ Since $-2\ne 1,$ $\lim_{h\to 0}\frac{f(1+h)-f(1)}{h}$ does not exist, and $f$ is not differentiable at $x=1.$

exercises.prompt:

$f(x)=\{\begin{array}{l}2x,x\le 1 \\ \frac{2}{x},x\gt 1\end{array}$

answer.solution:
a.

b. $\lim_{h\to 0^{-}}\frac{f(1+h)-f(1)}{h}=\lim_{h\to 0^{-}}\frac{2(1+h)-2}{h}=\lim_{h\to 0^{-}}\frac{2h}{h}=\lim_{h\to 0^{-}}2=2$ $\begin{array}{rl}\lim_{h\to 0^{+}}\frac{f(1+h)-f(1)}{h} & =\lim_{h\to 0^{+}}\frac{\frac{2}{1+h}-\frac{2}{1}}{h} \\ & =\lim_{h\to 0^{+}}\frac{\frac{2-2(1+h)}{1+h}}{h} \\ & =\lim_{h\to 0^{+}}\frac{-2h}{h(1+h)} \\ & =\lim_{h\to 0^{+}}\frac{-2}{1+h} \\ & =-2\end{array}$ $\lim_{h\to 0^{-}}\frac{f(1+h)-f(1)}{h}\ne \lim_{h\to 0^{+}}\frac{f(1+h)-f(1)}{h}$, so $\lim_{h\to 0}\frac{f(1+h)-f(1)}{h}$ does not exist.

a. $\frac{f(x+h)-f(x)}{h}$

b. $f^{\prime}(x)=\lim_{h\to 0}\frac{f(x+h)-f(x)}{h}$

$P(x)$ denotes the population of a city at time $x$ in years.

answer.solution: a. $\frac{P(x+h)-P(x)}{h}$ is the average rate of change of the city’s population over the $h$ years from year $x$ to year $x+h,$ in people per year. b. $P^{\prime}(x)$ is the instantaneous rate of change of the population at time $x,$ the rate at which the population is growing or shrinking in that year, in people per year.

exercises.prompt:
Suppose the total profit of a company is $y=P(x)$ thousand dollars when $x$ units of an item are sold.

a. What does $\frac{P(b)-P(a)}{b-a}$ for $0\lt a\lt b$ measure, and what are the units?

b. What does $P^{\prime}(x)$ measure, and what are the units?

c. Suppose that $P^{\prime}(30)=5,$ what is the approximate change in profit if the number of items sold increases from $30\;\text{to}\;31?$

answer.solution: a. $\frac{P(b)-P(a)}{b-a}$ is the average rate of change of profit as sales rise from $a$ to $b$ units, the average profit earned on each of those $b-a$ units, in thousands of dollars per unit. b. $P^{\prime}(x)$ is the instantaneous rate of change of profit when $x$ units are sold, approximately the profit from selling one more unit, in thousands of dollars per unit. c. Increasing sales from $30$ to $31$ units changes profit by about $P^{\prime}(30)\cdot 1=5$ thousand dollars, an increase of about ＄5000.

exercises.prompt:
True or False? Justify the answer with a proof or a counterexample.

Every function has a derivative.

answer.solution: False.

exercises.prompt:
True or False? Justify the answer with a proof or a counterexample.

A continuous function has a continuous derivative.

answer.solution: False. The function $f(x)=|x|$ is continuous everywhere, but it has no derivative at $0:$ the limits of $\frac{|x|}{x}$ from the left and the right are $-1$ and $1.$ So a continuous function need not have a derivative at every point, let alone a continuous derivative.

exercises.prompt:
True or False? Justify the answer with a proof or a counterexample.

A continuous function has a derivative.

answer.solution: False

exercises.prompt:
True or False? Justify the answer with a proof or a counterexample.

If a function is differentiable, it is continuous.

answer.solution: True. If $f$ is differentiable at $a,$ then $\lim_{x\to a}f(x)=\lim_{x\to a}\left(\frac{f(x)-f(a)}{x-a}\cdot (x-a)+f(a)\right)=f^{\prime}(a)\cdot 0+f(a)=f(a),$ so $f$ is continuous at $a;$ this is the theorem Differentiability Implies Continuity.
